newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durable goods orders fell unexpectedly in December.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durable goods orders fell unexpectedly in December.

text.p: Orders for costly manufactured goods dropped unexpectedly in December, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday, primarily because of a steep decline in demand for communications equipment.
New orders for durable goods fell 1.7 percent in December to a seasonally adjusted $168.99 billion, sharply contrary to Wall Street economists' forecasts of a 1.2 percent pickup in orders.
Shipments of finished manufactured products also weakened in December and order backlogs were flat.
The December decline followed a matching revised 1.7 percent drop in November orders -- the first back-to-back monthly decreases since January and February last year.

"It seems the story with orders right along has been supportive of a moderate growth economy," William Griggs, managing director of Griggs & Santow Inc., said. "This report doesn't change the very moderate uptrend in orders and in fact underscores the softness in the economy."

The department said that for the full year 1996 durable goods orders increased 5.5 percent to $2.03 trillion. Down from a 7.2 percent rise in 1995, it was the weakest gain since a 5.4 percent rise in 1993.
Some analysts saw a bright side, however.

"There are some signs within the report that suggest it's not as weak as it appears on the surface -- such as primary metals up 2.2 percent, industrial machinery up 1.5 percent," Michael Niemira, an economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd., said. "It's not so uniform and the big part of this story is the electronic component category dropped 12.5 percent."

Orders for electronic and electrical equipment plunged 12.5 percent to $24.55 billion in December after a 10.2 percent November increase. Department officials said the falloff covered a range of goods from communications equipment to electronic components.

New orders for transportation equipment were flat at $42 billion in December after a 1 percent increase in November. The department said orders were down for new cars and parts and for aircraft and parts but that was offset by increased orders for ships, military tanks and railroad equipment.

Aircraft orders also were weak in November, though there are significant orders still in the pipeline. American Airlines has agreed to buy more than $6 billion of airplanes from Boeing Co. But the airline said making the order final was contingent on it reaching a new labour pact with its pilots.

Excluding transportation, durables orders fell last month by 2.2 percent after a big 2.6 percent decline in November. The department said it was the seventh monthly decrease in this category during 1996.

Orders for durable goods, items like cars and home appliances that are intended to last at least three years, can indicate the future strength of the manufacturing sector, which in turn weighs heavily on the overall economy.
Orders for defence goods, which experience wide monthly swings, fell 4.7 percent last month to $8.29 billion after a 62.1 percent increase in November.

Orders for non-defence capital goods, an indication of business investment in new equipment, were down 0.5 percent in December to $43.69 billion after declining 7.5 percent in November and 0.1 percent in October.
Shipments of durable goods, an indication of current demand, fell 0.8 percent to $168.77 billion after a 0.8 percent rise in November.
Unfilled orders were unchanged in December at $488.91 billion following a 0.3 percent gain in November.
Orders for industrial machinery, which includes computers, were up 1.5 percent to $32.03 billion in December after a 0.9 percent decline in November.
